questions.question: In a queue where jobs arrive and depart one at a time, the stationary-probability recursion reads $p(n+1)=\frac{\lambda(n)}{\mu(n+1)}\,p(n)$, with $p(n)$ the time-average probability of $n$ jobs. What does the rate $\mu(n+1)$ in this recursion measure?
options: Departures per unit of time spent in state $n$, which take the system down to $n-1$.
Departures per unit of time spent with $n+1$ jobs present, each leaving $n$ jobs behind.
Departures that leave $n$ jobs behind, counted per unit of total elapsed time.
The total rate at which the system enters state $n+1$, from below or from above.

questions.question: The recursion $p(n+1)=\frac{\lambda(n)}{\mu(n+1)}\,p(n)$ expresses every time-average probability $p(n)$ of a queue as a known multiple of $p(0)$. How is the value of $p(0)$ itself determined?
options: By setting $p(0)=1$, since the unnormalised weights start the recursion at $q(0)=1$.
By the level-crossing equation between states $0$ and $1$, which fixes $p(0)$ directly.
By requiring $\sum_{n\geq0}p(n)=1$, so $p(0)$ is the reciprocal of the total weight $G$.
By the long-run fraction of arriving jobs that find the system empty on arrival.

questions.question: In a queue with limited room, arrivals that find the system full are blocked and leave. In the stationary-probability recursion written as $r(n)\,p(n)=\mu(n+1)\,p(n+1)$, which rate should $r(n)$ be?
options: The entry rate $\lambda^{+}(n)$, which counts only the arrivals in state $n$ that join.
The arrival rate $\lambda(n)$, which counts every arrival in state $n$, blocked or not.
The blocking rate $\lambda(n)-\lambda^{+}(n)$ of arrivals in state $n$ that are refused.
The overall arrival rate $\lambda=\sum_{k}\lambda(k)p(k)$, the same in every state.

questions.question: The recursion $p(n+1)=\frac{\lambda(n)}{\mu(n+1)}\,p(n)$ for time-average probabilities is derived for systems in which jobs arrive and depart one at a time. Why does it fail for a server that serves jobs in batches of two?
options: Batch service times are not exponential, and the recursion requires exponential service times.
With batch service the arrival rate $\lambda(n)$ must vary with $n$, and the recursion needs a constant rate.
With batch service $p(n)$ becomes a fraction of departures, while the recursion uses time averages.
A batch departure from $n+1$ to $n-1$ crosses two levels at once, so the cut equation gains extra terms.

questions.question: A single-server queue has $\lambda(n)=\lambda$ for all $n\geq0$ and $\mu(n)=\mu$ for all $n\geq1$, with $\lambda=\mu$ and no limit on the number of jobs. What does the stationary-probability recursion give?
options: Plugging $\rho=1$ into $p(n)=(1-\rho)\rho^{n}$ gives the valid distribution $p(n)=0$ for every $n$.
All weights equal $q(n)=1$, the normalising sum diverges, and no probability distribution fits.
All weights equal $q(n)=1$, so $p(n)$ is the uniform distribution over the states $0,1,2,\dots$.
Up and down moves are equally fast, so $p(0)=\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $p(n)=2^{-(n+1)}$ for $n\geq0$.

questions.question: Customers arrive as a Poisson process with rate $9$ per hour at a single server that works at rate $\mu(n)=3$ per hour for $n\geq1$. A customer who finds $n$ customers present joins with probability $\frac{1}{n+1}$ and otherwise leaves. What is $p(2)/p(1)$ for the time-average probabilities?

For a queue with states $0,1,2,3$, the unnormalised weights from $q(0)=1$ and $q(n+1)=q(n)\lambda(n)/\mu(n+1)$ are $q(0),\dots,q(3)=1,\ \tfrac{1}{2},\ \tfrac{1}{2},\ \tfrac{1}{4}$. What is the time-average probability $p(0)$ of an empty system?

A queue has time-average probabilities $p(0),p(1),p(2),p(3)=0.4,\,0.3,\,0.2,\,0.1$ and never holds more than three jobs. What is $\mathbb{P}(L\geq2)$, the long-run fraction of time with at least two jobs present?

A queue has arrival rates $\lambda(0),\dots,\lambda(3)=6,4,3,5$ and departure rates $\mu(1),\dots,\mu(4)=2,4,6,8$, all per hour, with jobs moving one at a time. What is the ratio $p(3)/p(0)$ of the time-average probabilities?

Jobs arrive as a Poisson process with rate $10$ per hour at $3$ identical servers in parallel, each finishing jobs at rate $4$ per hour, so $\mu(n)=4\min(n,3)$. What is the ratio $p(3)/p(2)$ of the time-average probabilities?

In a queue whose arrival rate $\lambda(n)$ varies with the number of jobs $n$, the recursion has produced the time-average probabilities $p(n)$. Which expression gives $\pi(n)$, the long-run fraction of arriving jobs that find $n$ jobs present?
options: $\pi(n)=p(n)$, as for Poisson arrivals
$\pi(n)=\frac{\lambda(n)}{\sum_{k}\lambda(k)}$
$\pi(n)=\frac{\lambda(n)\,p(n)}{\mu(n+1)}$
$\pi(n)=\frac{\lambda(n)p(n)}{\sum_{k}\lambda(k)p(k)}$

questions.question: In a queue with single-unit jumps whose time-average probabilities $p(n)$ exist, every arrival rate $\lambda(n)$ and every departure rate $\mu(n)$ is doubled. What happens to the time-average probabilities $p(n)$ and to the mean sojourn time $\mathbb{E}[J]$?
options: $p(n)$ stays the same and $\mathbb{E}[J]$ is halved.
$p(n)$ stays the same and $\mathbb{E}[J]$ stays the same.
$p(n)$ shifts to higher $n$ and $\mathbb{E}[J]$ doubles.
$p(n)$ stays the same and $\mathbb{E}[J]$ doubles.

questions.question: To compute the time-average probabilities of a queue with infinitely many states, the weights $q(0)=1$, $q(n+1)=q(n)\lambda(n)/\mu(n+1)$ are computed up to a level $N$ and divided by $\sum_{n\leq N}q(n)$. How should $N$ be chosen?
options: Any $N$ works: dividing by $\sum_{n\leq N}q(n)$ makes the $p(n)$ add up to one, so they are exact.
Stop at the first $N$ with $q(N)<0.001$, since every weight beyond it is then negligible.
Raise $N$ until the $p(n)$ stop changing; this is valid only when $\sum_n q(n)$ is finite.
A large enough $N$ always works, also when $\sum_n q(n)$ diverges, since the truncated sum is finite.

questions.question: A queue has time-average probabilities $p(0),p(1),p(2)=0.4,\,0.4,\,0.2$, and jobs join at rates $\lambda(0)=4$, $\lambda(1)=2$ and $\lambda(2)=0$ per hour. Using Little's law, what is the mean sojourn time $\mathbb{E}[J]$ of a job that joins?
options: $12$ minutes
$20$ minutes
$24$ minutes
$15$ minutes

questions.question: Three machines each break down at rate $1$ per day while working, and one mechanic repairs broken machines one at a time at rate $2$ per day, all times exponential. With $L$ the number of broken machines, what is $\mathbb{E}[L]$?

A single server speeds up when busy: $\mu(1)=2$ and $\mu(n)=4$ for $n\geq2$, per hour. Jobs arrive at rate $\lambda(n)=3$ per hour in every state, with no limit on the number of jobs. What is the time-average probability $p(0)$?
options: No value: $\lambda(0)/\mu(1)=\tfrac{3}{2}>1$, so no distribution exists

questions.question: For a queue with single-unit jumps and no upper limit on the number of jobs, a student claims: if $\lambda(n)<\mu(n+1)$ for every $n\geq0$, the stationary-probability recursion always yields probabilities $p(n)$ that add up to one. Which assessment of this claim is correct?
options: True: $\lambda(n)<\mu(n+1)$ at every level is the level-by-level form of $\rho<1$, so the $M/M/1$ argument carries over.
True: the weights $q(n)$ then decrease strictly, so they tend to zero and their sum is finite.
False: if $\lambda(n)/\mu(n+1)=\frac{n+1}{n+2}$, then $q(n)=\frac{1}{n+1}$ and $\sum_n q(n)$ diverges.
False, but only when $\lambda(n)$ varies with $n$; with a constant arrival rate the claim holds.

questions.question: A single-server queue has Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda=0.5$ per minute and deterministic service times of exactly $1$ minute. A student sets $\mu(n)=1$ for all $n\geq1$ in the recursion and concludes $p(n)=(0.5)^{n+1}$. Which assessment is correct?
options: The recursion fails because jobs do not leave one at a time when service times are deterministic.
The conclusion is correct: $\mu(n)=1/\mathbb{E}[S]$ for any service distribution, so $p(n)=(1-\rho)\rho^n$.
The error is in $\lambda(n)$: Poisson arrivals give $\lambda(n)=\lambda$ only when service is also exponential.
The recursion holds, but $\mu(n+1)$ is a measured rate that equals $1/\mathbb{E}[S]$ only for exponential service.

questions.question: In an $M/M/\infty$ queue every arriving job gets its own server, with arrival rate $\lambda=2$ per hour and service rate $\mu=1$ per hour per job, so $\mu(n)=n\mu$. What is the time-average probability $p(0)$?
options: $\mathrm{e}^{-2}\approx0.135$
No value: $\lambda/\mu=2>1$, so no distribution exists
$\mathrm{e}^{-1/2}\approx0.607$

questions.question: A single-server queue with room for at most $2$ jobs (including the one in service) has Poisson arrivals at rate $2$ per hour and exponential service at rate $1$ per hour; arrivals that find $2$ jobs are blocked. What long-run fraction of arriving jobs is blocked?
